content: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is a genetic disorder that primarily affects the lungs, digestive system, and pancreas. Individuals with CF often experience malnutrition and delayed growth. Despite adequate nutritional supplementation, optimal growth is not always achieved. Recombinant human growth hormone (rhGH) has been proposed as a potential treatment to address these issues. This review evaluates the effectiveness and safety of rhGH therapy in improving lung function, quality of life, and clinical outcomes in children and young adults with CF. The review included eight trials involving 291 participants aged between 5 and 23 years. Seven trials compared standard-dose rhGH (approximately 0.3 mg/kg/week) to no treatment, while one trial compared placebo, standard-dose rhGH, and high-dose rhGH (0.5 mg/kg/week). Six trials lasted one year, and two lasted six months. The findings suggest that rhGH therapy may improve certain pulmonary function outcomes, but no significant differences were observed between standard-dose and high-dose rhGH. The evidence for these improvements is of low certainty due to inconsistencies across trials, the small number of participants, and the short duration of the studies. Anthropometric parameters, including height, weight, and lean body mass, showed improvement with rhGH therapy. Height improved across all comparisons, but improvements in weight and lean body mass were only observed with standard-dose rhGH compared to no treatment. The certainty of this evidence ranged from very low to low. There was some evidence of changes in fasting blood glucose levels with rhGH therapy, but these changes did not reach the clinical threshold for diabetes diagnosis in the short-duration trials. This finding highlights the importance of monitoring blood glucose levels in CF patients receiving rhGH therapy, as they are already at risk for CF-related diabetes. Pulmonary exacerbations showed some improvement with rhGH therapy, but the evidence was of low to very low certainty. No significant adverse effects were reported, but the small number of participants and short trial durations limit the reliability of these findings. One small trial provided inconsistent evidence regarding improvements in quality of life, and the certainty of this evidence was very low. Limited evidence from three trials suggested improvements in exercise capacity, but this was also of low certainty. None of the trials systematically evaluated the cost-effectiveness of rhGH therapy in terms of overall healthcare expenses. In conclusion, rhGH therapy appears to improve intermediate outcomes such as height, weight, and lean body mass in individuals with CF. Some pulmonary function measures showed moderate improvement, but the benefits were not consistent across all trials. Changes in blood glucose levels, while not leading to diabetes, underscore the need for careful monitoring in this population. No significant improvements in quality of life or clinical status were observed, likely due to the small sample sizes and short trial durations. Long-term, well-designed randomized controlled trials are necessary before rhGH therapy can be routinely recommended for individuals with CF.
